Background and Summary The City of Wilton Manors (City) has been notified of significant rate increases by its wholesale water and large user wastewater treatment provider, the City of Fort Lauderdale (FLL). FLL’s September 1, 2026 letter identified wholesale water rate increases of 21.12% for FY 2027 and 23.25% for FY 2028. For wastewater, the large user rate approved for FY 2027 reflects an 18% increase; FLL has not yet provided information on wastewater rate adjustments beyond FY 2027. The City's 2025 Utility Rate Study (Rate Study) identified a wholesale/large user pass-through approach to handle the annual rate changes from FLL. However, these rate increases are significantly higher than the City anticipated. The City engaged Raftelis to review the financial impacts of these FLL rate adjustments and evaluate alternatives to implementation of the full pass-through. Based on our review, Raftelis supports FY 2027 rate adjustments of 10.9% for water and 8.1% for wastewater. Funding Transfer for Fire Prevention Services Outsourcing Transition - Approve the requested budget transfer from Fire Department Salaries and Benefits to Professional Services to support the transition of in-house fire prevention services to an outside professional service. The transition eliminates four full-time equivalent (FTE) positions, representing approximately $369,427 in annual salary and benefit expenditures. Transferring these savings to Professional Services allows the Department to fund a portion of the contracted prevention services while reducing long-term personnel costs and maintaining continuity of service. This approach provides greater operational flexibility, reduces administrative and staffing burdens, and allows the Department to align resources with current service delivery needs.

City Manager Abbate stated that on October 5, 2026, a significant water main break occurred at Garden Street and southbound US 1, requiring emergency repairs and road closures. Without the addition of the drain-down piping, the filters are limited to slowly draining through the filter media, which would extend the necessary time that the system must be taken offline to prepare for backwash operation, and prevent the efficient operation of the system. Per direction in Requests for Information (RFI) 501 and 502, one run of four-inch and six-inch drain-down piping will be provided connecting from each pressure filter to the filter effluent-to-waste line, for a total of four runs. One six-inch electrically-actuated butterfly valve will be provided on each piping run. Electrical and instrumentation/control system improvements will be provided to accommodate the drain-down system addition. The City issued Invitation to Bid (ITB) No. 2026-10 for the Tidal Valve Program on July 9, 2026, with bids opened on August 20, 2026. The project generally includes installation of inline backflow check valves at stormwater outfalls throughout the City, together with associated drainage structure modifications, pipe cleaning and repairs, pollution-retardant baffles, roadway and landscape restoration, and other related work. outgoing_grants.title: Evans Park Renovation – Officially Awarded The City has received an official $1.5 million LWCF grant award for the Evans Park Renovation Project, which ranked 3rd statewide. Evans Park is one of Mount Dora's most popular waterfront destinations for residents and visitors. However, the park currently lacks basic amenities, including public restrooms and supporting infrastructure. These limitations impact everyday park use and require the City to rent equipment or secure sponsorships to provide temporary amenities during special events. The $3 million renovation project will address these longstanding needs through the addition of permanent restrooms, a new outdoor amphitheater, waterfront trail, picnic and gathering areas, and other park improvements. These improvements will enhance the everyday experience for residents while providing the infrastructure needed to better accommodate community events and reduce the City's reliance on temporary facilities.

The project will include parcel acquisition and the reconstruction and improvement of Main Street, including roadway and drainage improvements to enhance the corridor’s safety, functionality, and resilience. The project will serve a predominantly Low- and Moderate-Income (LMI) community and address vulnerabilities identified following Hurricanes Helene and Milton. Summary: Over November 1 – 2, 2026, Palm Beach County experienced a severe rainfall event resulting in flooding of residential communities and a declared disaster (Fall Flooding) per Executive Order 26-228. The Department of Housing and Economic Development (HED) has identified $2,000,000 in SHIP Program Income which can be made available through the proposed FDAP to offer direct financial assistance to income-eligible homeowners who suffered damages to homestead property caused by the Fall Flooding disaster event. The statute defines that term, in part, as follows: “Gift,” for purposes of ethics in government and financial disclosure required by law, means that which is accepted by a donee or by another on the donee’s behalf, or that which is paid or given to another for or on behalf of a donee, directly, indirectly, or in trust for the donee’s benefit or by any other means, for which equal or greater consideration is not given within 90 days[.] The City’s prohibition reaches gifts of any value. The relevant question is therefore the character and source of the benefit, rather than whether the amount attributable to an employee falls below a monetary threshold. They do not establish a blanket exception for benefits merely routed through a City account. The City must exercise actual control, and the arrangement must not serve as a means for a vendor to provide an indirect gift to a covered individual. Additionally, the Florida Commission previously provided guidance to the City of Tallahassee on a similar matter. The Commission concluded that event tickets purchased by the City as part of a sponsorship package and subsequently distributed to officials and employees were gifts to the officials and employees from the City. By contrast, complimentary tickets supplied by outside organizations to officials and employees but distributed through the City for their benefit were indirect gifts from the outside organizations. It has continued to serve the community and is now part of Hillsborough County's International Baccalaureate (IB) World School program. Another period of population growth during the 1980s led to the construction of Lewis Elementary School in 1985. Named after Dr. Roland Lewis, a longtime Temple Terrace resident and public servant, the school honors his contributions to local government an d education. Dr. Lewis served on the Temple Terrace City Council from 1955 to 1968 and subsequently served on the Hillsborough County School Board from 1968 to 1988. He was the first person in Hillsborough County to have a school named in his honor while still living. Background: The Indian River Lagoon National Estuary Program (IRLNEP) opened their request for proposals on October 15, 2026, for grant funding opportunities for the October 1, 2027, through September 30, 2028, fiscal year. The current IRLNEP request allows for proposal submittals in multiple Indian River Lagoon benefiting categories; Water Quality Restoration Projects, Habitat Restoration Projects, Community Based Restoration Projects and Science and Innovation Projects. Proposals must be submitted by December 14, 2026, to be eligible for the review and ranking. Staff is requesting Board of County Commissioner (BOCC) approval to submit relevant proposals under this funding opportunity.

Should a County proposal be accepted for an award of funding from the IRLNEP, staff from the respective Department will bring the recommended award of funding to the BOCC for consideration and acceptance.

Staff Recommendation: Staff recommends the Board of County Commissioners authorize the submittal of proposals for the Indian River Lagoon National Estuary Program's 2028 funding cycle. If awarded, staff will bring any grant award contracts back to the BOCC for acceptance and execution.

To: Historic Preservation Board From: Kyle Wilkes, Senior Planner Date: November 10, 2026 Re: Certificate of Appropriateness COA-26-0001 - Construction of a Church Thrift Store At 317 S Mary Street (Ak 1189799) Introduction: The St. Thomas Episcopal Church currently operates a church ministry thrift store at 211 S Mary Street. The church has entered into an agreement with the Lake County School Board to grant the church-owned land to Eustis Elementary. The School Board's planned campus improvements, which include both this property and the main campus, will require demolishing or relocating the existing building that contains the thrift store. St. Thomas is requesting a Certificate of Appropriateness to construct a new building to house the thrift store. The applicant has provided anticipated floor plans and sketch elevations. This COA requests only the Historic Preservation Board's approval for the new thrift store construction, as the existing thrift store at 211 S Mary Street is outside the Washington Avenue Historic District.

City Manager Abbate stated that on October 5, 2026, a significant water main break occurred at Garden Street and southbound US 1, requiring emergency repairs and road closures. Public Works crews replaced the damaged 6-inch water main, restoring water service by 9 p.m., and issued a boil water notice. The break caused extensive roadway damage, requiring emergency repairs by Masci General Contractors, Inc., under a $397,671 emergency purchase order. The intersection reopened on October 7, 2026 with final paving expected before the City Council meeting on October 13, 2026. The purchase order would be presented to Council for after-the-fact approval once final costs were confirmed.

N. Piggybacking The practice of procurement by one agency using the agreement of another agency is called piggybacking. The ability to piggyback onto an existing contract is not unlimited. The Subrecipient’s written procurement policy shall be submitted to the Division and shall allow for piggybacking. The existing contract shall contain language or other legal authority authorizing third parties to make purchases from the contract with the vendor’s consent. The terms and conditions of the new contract, including the Scope of Work, shall be substantially the same as those of the existing contract and approved by the Division. The piggyback contract shall not exceed the existing contract in scope or volume of goods or services. A Subrecipient shall not use the preexisting contract merely as a “basis to begin negotiations” for a broader or materially different contract. 17. Approve Piggyback Purchase for Administration East Building VAV Replacement Item Summary: Provides 76 new variable air volume (VAV) units for the Administration East Building. The existing units are more than 25 years old and have reached the end of their useful life. Replacing them will improve air quality, make the heating and cooling system more reliable, and improve overall building comfort. The work will be completed through Omnia Partners Contract No. 02-139 with Page Mechanical Group, LLC, a subsidiary of PremiStar, LLC, for $435,200. The cost includes equipment, installation, labor, materials, and removal of the old units. This planned and budgeted project will be funded through the General Fund. Using the piggyback method allows the County to take advantage of large-scale contract volume discounts and benefit from a shorter timeframe because a competitive procurement process has already been conducted. A market analysis was completed and the purchase under this contract will represent a savings of $3,443, or 0.785%.

This agreement will be 100% funded through FTA grant funds.

Consideration Background: The Arts and Entertainment Department rents portable toilets for Special Events at the Bandshell. The service is essential to ensuring the health and safety of people attending the events. Establishing a service agreement for the portable restrooms will allow the City to efficiently conduct the events. Public Works and Utilities Director Jennifer Spagnoli reported that during submittal coordination with the pressure filter vessel manufacturer, it was realized that four valved drain-down piping runs were not included in the original contract scope and should be added to facilitate the rapid draining of the filter vessels down to the top of media elevation to prepare for a backwash cycle. Without the addition of the drain-down piping, the filters are limited to slowly draining through the filter media, which would extend the necessary time that the system must be taken offline to prepare for backwash operation, and prevent the efficient operation of the system. Per direction in Requests for Information (RFI) 501 and 502, one run of four-inch and six-inch drain-down piping will be provided connecting from each pressure filter to the filter effluent-to-waste line, for a total of four runs. One six-inch electrically-actuated butterfly valve will be provided on each piping run. Electrical and instrumentation/control system improvements will be provided to accommodate the drain-down system addition. The City issued Invitation to Bid (ITB) No. 2026-10 for the Tidal Valve Program on July 9, 2026, with bids opened on August 20, 2026. The project generally includes installation of inline backflow check valves at stormwater outfalls throughout the City, together with associated drainage structure modifications, pipe cleaning and repairs, pollution-retardant baffles, roadway and landscape restoration, and other related work. Following review of the bids, Southern Underground Industries, Inc. was determined to be the lowest responsive and responsible bidder. Mr. Ennis reported that as part of the annual resurfacing program, the city evaluates the existing water, sewer, reclaimed and drainage facilities to ensure that no repairs are needed prior to the resurfacing of the roadway. As determined by pipe inspections, the existing drainage pipes within the following rights of way are in need of repair prior to resurfacing. Work Order No. 18 provides for the rehabilitation of approximately 2,200 linear feet of drainage pipes along Butler Street, Ferndale Avenue, Georgetown Avenue, Gulfview Drive, Leonard Weaver Boulevard, Stan Drive, Sherry Lane, and Veracruz Drive ranging in size between 15-inches to 48-inches, as further described in the exhibit provided. EXPLANATION: Congress appropriated funds through the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) Community Development Block Grant - Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) Program in response to the 2023 Hurricane Idalia (DR-4734-FL) and the 2024 Hurricane Helene (DR-4828- FL). Assistance for these disasters was appropriated on December 21, 2024, by the Disaster Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act of 2025. The City of St. Petersburg (City) was allocated $159,884,000 per the Allocation Announcement Notice (90 FR 4759) published on January 16, 2025. On June 12, 2025, City Council approved the CDBG-DR Action Plan for the use of the federal grant funds (Resolution No. 2025-327) which allocated $6,000,000 to the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program. HUD approved the City’s Action Plan in August 2025 and executed the City’s Grant Agreement in February 2026. Through extensive public input and Unmet Needs and Mitigation Needs Assessments in the Action Plan, the City determined the need to create the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program to address the increased need for essential community services as a result of the qualifying disasters. Re: Resolution Number 2026-113: Assignment of Commercial Contract and Addendum and Associated Budget Amendment Introduction: The City has an opportunity to acquire 44 Sharps Circle through assignment of the Commercial Contract and First Addendum between Hometown Property Investments, LLC (Assignor) and Lake Eustis MHP, LLC (Seller). The acquisition is subject to existing lawful tenancies, with any later closure, relocation or demolition requiring separate implementation under applicable law. Background: The subject property has been identified as a catalyst site in the Downtown Master Plan and is key to the future execution of that plan. The parcels are identified by the Lake County Property Appraiser as: • 11-19-26-0200-061-00000 and, • 11-19-26-0200-068-00000 The City has attempted to acquire these parcels historically and they are instrumental to the success of the waterfront activation component of the Downtown Master Plan. Negotiated Terms: The key provisions of the Assignment include: • Purchase Price: $10,000,000, with the deposits credited toward the purchase price and the remaining balance due at closing, subject to applicable adjustments and credits. • Deposit: $50,000 in

Statutory Requirements: The acquisition will proceed under Section 2-404 of the Eustis Code without using the public records exemption in Section 166.045, Florida Statutes. Two MAI appraisals are required before purchase. If the price exceeds their average, approval requires four affirmative votes at a public hearing with an opportunity for public input. Any necessary budget amendment will be adopted by resolution under Section 2-193 of the Code. Legal/Policy Analysis: The City Attorney has reviewed the proposed transaction which provides for: • Termination at the City’s sole discretion during the remaining Due Diligence Period by timely written notice. • Title and survey review and environmental inspections under the Contract and First Addendum. • Commission approval and Finance confirmation of appropriated funds available when due before City execution. • City Attorney written authorization before disbursement of the City’s closing funds. Upon effectiveness of the Assignment and Seller’s Consent, the City will assume Buyer’s rights, obligations, and liabilities under the Contract. The Agreement imposes no undue obligations and reflects standard municipal acquisition protections.

Public Hearing and Second Reading of Ordinance 1607 Adopting the Annual Modification and Update to the Capital Improvements Section of the City's Comprehensive Plan. Mayor Ross opened the Public Hearing. Marisa Robinson, Deputy Community Development Director , presented the second reading for the Annual Modification and Update to the Capital Improvements Section of the City's Comprehensive Plan. She recapped what the Hillsborough Planning Commission presented at the previous Council Meeting. The CIS is required by state statute to be updated annually by ordinance. The Planning Commission staff coordinates with the Finance and Public Works departments to obtain information on the capital improvement program. The CIP programs are just under $109 million for fiscal years 27 through 31, ranging in nine different program areas. The planning commission then extrapolates the data from the CIS with projects affecting levels of service; 39% going to repair and replacement, 3% to future growth, and 59% to eliminate deficiencies.
